question: The 2025 annual report of the European Ombudsman, Teresa Anjinho1, mentions an inquiry being opened into the development of EU standards for artificial intelligence. That inquiry raises questions about the creation of the standards and the people working on them.

With the technical standards developed as part of implementing the AI Act being likely to have significant consequences for French and EU businesses, administrations and citizens, the rules in question must surely be developed in a clear manner to increase public trust. In view of the above: 1.

How does the Commission ensure transparency in the process of developing EU standards for artificial intelligence, particularly as regards access to information on participants and their contributions?
How does it make sure there is balanced representation of the different stakeholders participating in the work, including SMEs, researchers, civil society organisations and Member States?
Does it think that the rules could slow down the development of AI in the EU and increase its dependence on the US and China?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) European Standardisation Organisations (ESOs) are bound by the provisions on transparency of the Regulation on Standardisation1. If these provisions are not met, the Commission can decide not to cite offered harmonised standards in the Official Journal.

There are however no legal requirements on ESOs to disclose to the public information on participants and their contributions, but this information is available for participants of the respective technical committee. Sharing information on specific contributions goes beyond the reporting obligations of ESOs to the Commission.

The Commission’s request to the ESOs to develop harmonised standards for the AI Act2 contains, in line with the Regulation on Standardisation3, requirements to facilitate the appropriate representation and effective participation of relevant stakeholders. The ESOs are required to report on the fulfilment of this and other requirements to the Commission every three months.

The AI Act lays down a single set of rules for AI in the EU, creating a level playing field for all companies that want to do business in the EU. Only AI systems classified as high-risk AI need to fulfil the requirements for high-risk AI systems.

Standards play a key role to provide technical solutions to providers to ensure compliance with the AI Act, to promote innovation as well as competitiveness and growth in the single market. All companies that aim to develop trustworthy AI can benefit from using these standards. Standards will thus help the development of AI in the EU.
1 Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2012 on

European standardisation, amending Council Directives 89/686/EEC and 93/15/EEC and Directives 94/9/EC, 94/25/EC, 95/16/EC, 97/23/EC, 98/34/EC, 2004/22/EC, 2007/23/EC, 2009/23/EC and 2009/105/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Decision 87/95/EEC and Decision No 1673/2006/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council Text with EEA relevance.

2 Commission Implementing Decision C(2025)3871 on a standardisation request to the European Committee for Standardisation and the European Committee for Electrotechnical Standardisation as regards high-risk AIsystems in support of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Implementing Decision C(2023)3215.
